CERN

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we visit the world's largest and most respected scientific research centre

Unique Selling Point:
The internet, GPS satellites and mobile phones - these are just some of the inventions to have come out of CERN. But it was the discovery of the "God particle" - proof that an energy field fills the universe - that was the greatest discovery in the history of Physics.

Summary:
We visit CERN and meet some of the physicists from South Africa that are helping to breach the barriers of science.

Press Release:


CERN
Geneva, Switzerland is the home of CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. It’s here where physicists, scientists and engineers from around the world, are
probing the fundamental structure of the universe. CERN also hosts the Large Hadron Collider where the existence of the Higgs boson particle was confirmed. Carte
Blanche meets some extraordinary Southern African scientists who are at the forefront of scientific discovery.

Script:


CERN

V/O: On the outskirts of Geneva, sitting astride the Franco-Swiss border is CERN. With an annual budget of $1 billion, it’s the world’s largest and most respected centre for Physics research.

Link: If you want to be a top scientist, the European Organisation for Nuclear Research, or CERN, is the place you want to be. Some of the greatest minds in the world are right here, looking for some very complicated answers.

V/O: What is the Universe made of? How did it start? These are questions posed by CERN, using the world’s largest instruments to study the smallest particles of matter. And this is where they made the greatest discovery in the history of Physics: the so-called God particle.

Claire: They are really experiments that are pushing the boundaries of science, and technology, and engineering.

V/O: Dr Claire Lee is a South African particle physicist who works on one of the four big experiments at the LHC, or Large Hadron Collider.

Claire: It’s a 27 Km long underground tunnel and in this tunnel you have 1200 magnets, all the way around and the job of those magnets is to bend protons and the reason why we need magnets to bend protons is because normally protons like to go in a straight line and the reason why we need really big magnets to bend the protons is because we need to make these protons go really fast. The main goal of the LHC and the accelerator is to speed up these protons and then to smash them together.

V/O: These collisions replicate the moment of the Big Bang. The protons, travelling close to the speed of light, in opposite directions, collide at 4 separate points along the 27km tunnel. These are the 4 different experiments on the LHC, and Claire works at the ATLAS Experiment. With a Master’s degree from Wits University and a PhD from the University of Johannesburg, Claire has been with the ATLAS team since 2011.

Claire: South Africa is a member of the ATLAS Experiment and the Alice Experiment. So, once you are a member of an experiment you are allowed to send students to work on that experiment.

Chilufya: I attended a school that CERN had started to bring CERN to Africa. And it’s called the African School of Physics and it was held in 2010, first in Stellenbosch. So, I attended that and I was learning about particle Physics for the very first time, and I heard about CERN and I was really intrigued.

V/O: Zambian UCT student Chilufya Mwewa has been awarded one of only three PhD grants from the ATLAS Detector.

Chilufya: There are so many skills that we learn here. I hope that I can learn some of those skills to maybe bring about some kind of development in Zambia. Maybe improve the education system, or eradicate poverty.

Joshua: We have a SA CERN group with multiple universities in South Africa.

V/O: Joshua Smith is another PhD student working at ATLAS.

Joshua: For the first week, you walk around not really knowing what to do with yourself so it really is a mind-blowing experience and then you realize that you’re surrounded by Nobel prize laureates, it’s really quite humbling.

V/O: The day we visited CERN the proton beam was up and running, making it impossible to take us underground. But we were shown a life-size replica of the CMS Experiment.

Link: This is one of the four experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. It’s not actually the biggest, but it is the heaviest at 14 000 tons.

Derek: Tell us about ATLAS?

Claire: ATLAS is like a gigantic digital camera. It’s an experiment that is built to detect all of the stuff that comes out of a proton/proton collision. What we are really interested in is what happens after those collisions. Do we get a Higgs boson? Do we get just a bunch of particles spraying out in different directions? What happens, how often does each of these things happen?

Derek: Just like the police arriving at the scene of an accident?

Claire: Exactly.

V/O: In 1964 CERN physicist Peter Higgs proposed that there was an energy field that permeated the entire Universe. This became known as the Higgs Field.

Claire: Peter Higgs was the only person who came up with the idea that there should be a particle to go along with it, so that’s really why we call it the Higgs Boson and the Higgs Field.

V/O: On the 4th of July 2012 CERN announced the discovery of the Higgs boson. It was the missing piece of the puzzle for particle physics.

Claire: Both the ATLAS and CMS experiments announced our discovery of a new boson that looked and smelt and acted like what had been predicted to be the Higgs boson. We both had the same signal that showed up in the same way.

Derek: Independently?

Claire; Independently, which is what gave us such confidence that this was the real thing. Peter Higgs was in the audience at the seminar and he got some tears in his eyes to see the theory that he proposed back in 1964 finally be proven.

Higgs: Well I would like to add my congratulations to everybody involved in this tremendous achievement. For me it’s really an incredible thing that it’s happened in my lifetime.

Claire: So, we’ve got our complete puzzle which describes everything that we know of in the universe. Except all of that sums up to only about 5% of everything that actually exists in the universe. So, there’s 95% of the universe we don’t actually know about.

Derek: Claire this really is fascinating. Do you look at the world in a different way?

Claire: It can put things in perspective sometimes when people are going crazy about what this latest celebrity is wearing and you’re wondering about what the extra 95% of the universe is.

V/O: Claire’s husband Chris Lee works in CERN as Coordinator of the ATLAS Computer Centre.

Chris: When the experiment runs, there is a possibility of 600 million collisions per second. Now in the ATLAS Detector for example each event is 1.6 megabytes. At 600 million collisions per second we can’t store all that information, so we have a highly-developed trigger system which goes through the events as they’re coming out of the Detector, and selects ones which they believe are interesting, and throws away most of the data. I believe the Data Centre right here processes one petabyte of data a day.

V/O: A petabyte is equal to a million gigabytes, but even a data centre as big as this cannot store that much information.

Chris: From here, it is put together in special files, and then it is sent to sites around the world. There are currently more than 160 different computing sites all over the world which all share their computing resource power with CERN. Something like 536 000 computing cores at this point in time.

Link: About a quarter of a million visitors are attracted to CERN and its iconic symbols every year, and they get an over view of what is not just lofty science but research that leads to practical applications that we use in our everyday lives.

Chris: CERN has always been an open source project – things like the worldwide web which was developed by Tim Berners-Lee here at CERN as well. That was completely done and shared with the world, and everybody today uses it. That was initially developed as a project for scientists to share information.

Claire: Every time we’ve made a fundamental discovery about how the universe works like with general relativity or quantum mechanics, we have had technological spinoffs that had come up many years later as a result of this, for example, GPS tracking satellites and semiconductor devices like our cell phones.

Derek: But you do believe there is a space for fundamental research?

Claire: Of course. It’s allowing people to have those passions and to work on those passions without having to worry about a certain result down the line. That freedom is actually what allows people to be creative and what allows the discoveries to be made that then end up having a domino effect later on. It’s fundamentally important to realize that pure research is not just a privilege but it’s a necessity even for third world countries.

V/O: The CERN site is like a huge university with no undergraduates. Thousands of scientists are gathered from all over the world, including Africa.

Hilary: What excites me about being here at CERN is the concept of having radio-active isotopes which are very short-lived – it changes the way we do experiments.

V/O: Zimbabwean physicist Dr Hilary Masenda is a visiting lecturer from Wits University.

Hilary: Doing a simple measurement in a home lab at Wits, it will take up to 2 weeks or a month doing measurements. But here at CERN, because they are short-lived isotopes you can do measurements in 3 minutes. So, it sort of changes the dynamics.

Claire: It's an amazing experience because you are at the world's leading scientific laboratory, and you’re interacting with thousands of people from all around the world - on these huge scales - of collaborating with 3000 people.

V/O: And the ATLAS collaboration is painstakingly searching for every puzzle piece in the universe.

Claire: Before the Higgs discovery, we knew there was a piece and we knew the shape of the piece, now we have no idea how many pieces there are, we’re really not 100% sure if there really are pieces…and that’s why the search is on.
